claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability is governed by a thin surface oxide passivation layer.
The surface oxide layer acts as a barrier to atomic diffusion and elemental segregation.
The as-synthesized nanoparticles have minimal native oxidation.
Mild controlled oxidation will form a thin, uniform surface oxide layer.
Processing in a reducing environment will keep the comparison nanoparticles essentially oxide-free.
The pre-formed oxide layer decreases high-temperature surface diffusion.
The pre-formed oxide layer inhibits interdiffusion among the constituent metal atoms.
Decreased atomic mobility reduces elemental segregation.
Decreased atomic mobility reduces phase separation.
Decreased atomic mobility reduces structural degradation under thermal stress.
Oxide-passivated nanoparticles will retain greater structural integrity than oxide-free nanoparticles under otherwise identical high-temperature conditions.
Oxide-passivated nanoparticles will retain greater chemical homogeneity and exhibit less phase segregation and elemental demixing than oxide-free nanoparticles.
The passivation mechanism is effective only while the oxide layer remains stable and does not thicken excessively or degrade.
Adverse chemical interactions with the service environment can override the passivation effect.
Gas interactions may influence nanoparticle structural evolution.
Intrinsic nanoparticle composition variations may influence structural evolution.
